'''Ania Bleszynski Jayich''' is an American experimental physicist most known for developing novel sensing techniques that shed light on [[biological]], [[condensed matter]], and [[quantum mechanical]] systems.<ref name=CNSI>{{cite web|title=California NanoSystems Institute UCSB|url=https://www.cnsi.ucsb.edu/news/1024|website=University of California, Santa Barbara|accessdate=18 September 2019}}</ref> Bleszynski Jayich is the Bruker Endowed Chair in Science and Engineering in the Department of Physics at the [[University of California, Santa Barbara]] and Associate Director of the campus's Materials Research Lab.<ref name=APS>{{cite web|title=APS Author Profile|url=https://physics.aps.org/authors/ania_bleszynski_jayich|website=American Physical Society|accessdate=18 September 2019}}</ref>

==Biography==
Bleszynski Jayich was raised in [[Thousand Oaks, California]].<ref name=LA>{{cite web|title=It's All Academic|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1997-04-24-sp-51737-story.html|website=Los Angeles Times|date=24 April 1997 |accessdate=18 September 2019}}</ref> As the daughter of two physicists, she decided at an early age to dedicate her life to the subject as well.<ref name=YD>{{cite web|title=Researcher Wins a Prestigious Fellowship for Women Scientists|url=https://yaledailynews.com/blog/2008/12/04/postdoc-wins-women-in-science-fellowship/|website=Yale Daily News|date=4 December 2008 |accessdate=18 September 2019}}</ref> Bleszynski Jayich was also an elite tennis player growing up; she held the rank of No. 1 singles tennis in the United States for athletes 18-and-under.<ref name=LA/>  Bleszynski Jayich attended [[Stanford University]] and received a B.S. with honors in 2000 as a double major in mathematics and computational science, and physics.<ref name=YD/> There, she conducted research in a collaboration with Stanford, NASA, and the Lockheed Corporation.<ref name=LA/> [[Steven Chu]] supervised her undergraduate thesis at Stanford, which was recognized with an award for best honors thesis in physics.<ref name=YD/> At the time, Bleszynski Jayich explained her interest: “I love the problem-solving process. The more you learn, the more of these things you can use as tools in the learning process.”<ref name=LA/> At Stanford, Bleszynski Jayich was named most outstanding sophomore athlete and selected as an NCAA All-American for four years.<ref name=YD/>

Bleszynski Jayich pursued her graduate studies in physics at Harvard under the supervision of Robert Westervelt. Her PhD thesis, on the topic "Imaging Electrons in Nanoscale Structures" (2006), applied scanning probe techniques to illuminate the structure of quantum dots in nanowires.<ref name=thesis>{{cite web|title=Imaging Electrons in Nanoscale Structures|url=https://meso.seas.harvard.edu/theses/bleszynski.pdf|website=Harvard University|accessdate=18 September 2019}}</ref> Afterwards, as a postdoctoral researcher at Yale University, Bleszynski Jayich worked with [[Jack Harris (physicist)|Jack Harris]] to perform the first measurements of a counter-intuitive quantum mechanical effect in which rings of normal metal conductors are expected to support persistent currents.<ref name=rings>{{cite journal|title=Persistent Currents in Normal Metal Rings
|url=https://www.science.org/doi/abs/10.1126/science.1178139|journal=Science|year=2009 |doi=10.1126/science.1178139 |accessdate=20 September 2019|last1=Bleszynski-Jayich |first1=A. C. |last2=Shanks |first2=W. E. |last3=Peaudecerf |first3=B. |last4=Ginossar |first4=E. |last5=von Oppen |first5=F. |author6-link=Leonid Glazman |last6=Glazman |first6=L. |last7=Harris |first7=J. G. E. |volume=326 |issue=5950 |pages=272–275|pmid=19815772 |bibcode=2009Sci...326..272B |s2cid=37548342 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Her work, which was recognized in 2008 with a [[L'Oréal-UNESCO For Women in Science Award]],<ref name=YD/> identified the minuscule magnetic fields these currents produce by using ultra-sensitive cantilever beams. Next, she expanded her postdoctoral collaboration to include [[Mikhail Lukin]] of Harvard to couple [[nitrogen-vacancy center]]s in diamond to nanomechanical resonators.<ref name=nv>{{cite journal|title=Coherent Sensing of a Mechanical Resonator with a Single-Spin Qubit|journal=Science|year=2012 |doi=10.1126/science.1216821 |last1=Kolkowitz |first1=Shimon |last2=Bleszynski Jayich |first2=Ania C. |last3=Unterreithmeier |first3=Quirin P. |last4=Bennett |first4=Steven D. |last5=Rabl |first5=Peter |last6=Harris |first6=J. G. E. |last7=Lukin |first7=Mikhail D. |volume=335 |issue=6076 |pages=1603–1606 |pmid=22362881 |s2cid=5459266 |doi-access=free |bibcode=2012Sci...335.1603K }}</ref><ref name=mrl>{{cite web|title=Associate Director Profile, Ania Jayich|url=https://www.mrl.ucsb.edu/people/faculty-administration/ania-jayich|website=UCSB Materials Research Laboratory|accessdate=20 September 2019}}</ref>

In 2010, Bleszynski Jayich joined the physics faculty of [[University of California, Santa Barbara]].<ref name=mrl/> The Jayich Lab is the Quantum Sensing and Imaging Group at UCSB, specializing in quantum effects on the nanoscale. Of particular interest to the Jayich Lab is the nanoscale imaging of spin and charge in condensed matter systems. These experiments have applications in quantum and classical computing and biology. Bleszynski Jayich is a principal investigator of the first [[National Science Foundation]] Quantum Foundry, based at UCSB. The UC Santa Barbara NSF Quantum Foundry is a major initiative (20 faculty, $25M) seeking to develop new materials with quantum applications.<ref name=nsf>{{cite web|title=A Quantum Leap|url=https://www.news.ucsb.edu/2019/019626/quantum-leap|website=The Current, UCSB News|date=16 September 2019 |accessdate=20 September 2019}}</ref>

==Honors and awards==
* NSF CAREER Award, 2014<ref name=APS/>
* Presidential Early Career Award for Scientists and Engineers (PECASE), 2012<ref name=APS/>
* Air Force Office of Scientific Research Young Investigator Award, 2010<ref name=APS/>
* L’Oreal Postdoctoral Fellowship for Women in Science (2008)<ref name=YD/>
